text: Every attack in this chapter — poisoning, supply chain risk, backdoors — depends on the same opening move: an attacker gets unverified data into a pipeline that feeds a model. Data provenance is the direct countermeasure. It means tracking exactly where every piece of training data came from, who collected or modified it, and when, so unexplained or unauthorized changes become visible instead of silently flowing into the next training run. It's the same chain-of-custody idea used in digital forensics, and the same idea Lesson 10 applied to software dependencies — just pointed at datasets instead.

In practice, that means treating a dataset like source code: versioned, diffable, and reviewable before it's used. Tools like DVC, lakeFS, and dataset tracking built into MLflow let a team see exactly what changed between one training run's data and the next, the same way git diff shows what changed in code. On top of that, real validation frameworks check a dataset automatically before it's allowed into training. TensorFlow Data Validation compares schema and distribution statistics across versions and flags drift. Great Expectations lets a team write explicit rules about value ranges and allowed categories, and fails the pipeline automatically when a batch violates them.

Neither tool was built specifically to catch poisoning, but both catch its most common symptom: data that doesn't look statistically like what came before, whether the cause is an attacker or an ordinary upstream data-quality bug. And the model and dataset cards from Lesson 10 work the same way internally — documenting a dataset's source and limitations at the point it's approved for training turns a later question like 'did this data change, and who signed off on it' into something answerable instead of guesswork.

Put the whole chapter together and you get a practical checklist. Know your sources before approving a dataset or model for use. Version your data so changes are diffable, not silent. Validate automatically, every single run, not just during occasional review. Keep a holdout set the pipeline never writes to, so you always have a clean baseline — including for the backdoor-detection techniques from Lesson 11. And control and audit who can write to training data, the same way you'd control access to any other sensitive system.

That closes out data poisoning and training-time attacks. Chapter 4 shifts from attacks on what a model learns to attacks on a model that's already deployed — starting with model extraction, where an attacker tries to steal a working copy of your model through nothing but its own public API.
